name: Sarangkot
tagline: Pokhara's sunrise ridge and paragliding launch above Phewa
meta_description: Sarangkot above Pokhara: sunrise over Dhaulagiri, Annapurna and Manaslu, tandem paragliding, the hike up from Lakeside and the ridge walk to old Kaskikot.
summary: Sarangkot is a 1,600 m ridge just northwest of Pokhara, now Ward 18 of the city. It is the classic sunrise point for the Annapurna range, with Dhaulagiri and Manaslu at either end, and the launch site for Pokhara's tandem paragliding flights over Phewa Lake.
intro: From Lakeside, Sarangkot is the green ridge you see above the north end of Phewa, about 800 m higher than the lake. Drive up in 30–40 minutes before dawn and you stand on a viewing tower as the light moves along the range: Dhaulagiri in the west, Annapurna South, Annapurna I and Machhapuchhre in front, and on very clear days Manaslu far to the east. Below you, Pokhara and the lake come out of the mist.

Later in the morning the same ridge fills with paragliders. Thermals rising off the sunny slope make it one of the best tandem launch sites in Asia, and on good days dozens of canopies circle over the lake before landing at the north end of Lakeside. If you would rather walk, footpaths climb from Lakeside and from the old bazaar side through forest and village terraces. Walking up takes two hours or a little more, and it is the best way to see the farms and houses that the sunrise crowd drives straight past.

Sarangkot is still a village. Brahmin, Chhetri, Gurung and Magar families farm the slopes and run homestays and small lodges along the road. Stay a night and the sunrise needs no alarm at 4:30 am; you just step out of the door. Then walk the ridge west towards Kaskikot, the hill that gave the Kaski kingdom and today's district its name. Half a day is enough for sunrise and a short walk; a night on the ridge turns it into something slower and better.

story.title: A fort ridge turned sunrise point
paras: Kot means fort in Nepali, and the hills around Pokhara are full of kot names: Sarangkot, Kaskikot, Pumdikot and, further east, Nuwakot. They date from the centuries when the Gandaki basin was split into small rival kingdoms and every ridge with a view of the valley was worth holding. Kaskikot, a little further west on the same line of hills, was the seat of the kings of Kaski, who ruled Pokhara's valley until the Gorkha state absorbed them in 1786.

For most of its history Sarangkot was a farming village of terraced millet, maize and rice, with paths down to the Phewa shore and to the trade route towards Baglung. Villagers carried produce down to Pokhara's bazaar on their backs. The hike up from the Pokhara–Baglung road at Miruwa takes about 90 minutes, and for generations that was the only way. Water came from springs on the slope, and the ridge's forests supplied fodder and firewood. Houses were built of stone and mud with thatched or slate roofs, many of which have since given way to concrete and tin.

The road, the sunrise tower and the paragliding came in the past few decades, and the village changed with them: guesthouses on the ridge, tea stalls at the viewpoint, and pilots' launch strips cut into the grassy slope. In 2015 Sarangkot was merged into Pokhara as Ward 18. The farms are still there just off the road, and so is the view that made the ridge worth defending. Early in the morning, before the taxis arrive, it still feels like a farming village with a very good view.

people: Sarangkot's households are a mix of Brahmin, Chhetri, Gurung and Magar families, many with relatives in the Gurkhas or working abroad. Most still farm maize, millet and vegetables on terraces, while those along the ridge road run guesthouses, tea stalls and small shops for sunrise visitors. Some young men from the village now work as paragliding ground crew and pilots.

untold.fact: Sarangkot was a separate village development committee until 2015, when it was merged into Pokhara as Ward 18; at the 1991 census it had about 5,060 people in 1,010 households.
Kaskikot, the hill west of Sarangkot along the same ridge, was the seat of the old Kaski kingdom that gave Kaski District its name; it is now Ward 24 of Pokhara.
Three of the world's ten highest mountains can be seen from Sarangkot on a clear day: Dhaulagiri (8,167 m), Annapurna I (8,091 m) and Manaslu (8,163 m).

local_words.meaning: Fort or hilltop stronghold, the ending of many ridge names

taste.name: Sel roti and milk tea
taste.text: Ring-shaped rice-flour bread, deep-fried until crisp outside and soft inside, eaten with sweet milk tea. Tea stalls at the Sarangkot viewpoint fry it fresh before dawn for sunrise crowds, and homestays serve it at breakfast, especially around Dashain and Tihar when every family makes it.

facts: Sunrise over the Annapurnas, tandem paragliding

highlights.title: Sunrise along the range
highlights.text: From the viewing tower the first light touches Dhaulagiri, then Annapurna South, Annapurna I and Machhapuchhre, and on clear days Manaslu. October to February give the cleanest views; arrive 30 minutes before sunrise. Tea stalls open before dawn.

highlights.title: Tandem paragliding
highlights.text: Launch from Sarangkot's grass slope with a licensed pilot and ride thermals over Phewa for 20–30 minutes or longer, landing at Lakeside. Morning flights after 10 am usually have the best lift. Book with a registered operator.

highlights.title: Walking up from Lakeside
highlights.text: A forest and village trail climbs about 800 m from the north end of Lakeside in 2–2.5 hours, passing terraces and farmhouses. It is the way villagers have always come and gone. Start in the afternoon to arrive for sunset.

highlights.title: Ridge walk to Kaskikot
highlights.text: Follow the ridge west through farmland to Kaskikot, the old seat of the Kaski kings, with Phewa below on one side and the Annapurnas on the other. Allow about two hours one way. Carry water and a hat.

highlights.title: A night in a ridge guesthouse
highlights.text: Sleep on the ridge and wake to the range from your window. Evenings are cool and quiet, with Pokhara's lights spread below and the snow peaks catching the last pink light. Book ahead in October and November.

how_to_reach.text: Taxis and private cars drive from Lakeside to the Sarangkot viewpoint car park in 30–40 minutes on a paved road via the Bindhyabasini side, then a short climb on steps. Book a sunrise taxi the night before; drivers wait and bring you back. Paragliding operators drive clients to the launch in their own jeeps.

Trails climb from the north end of Lakeside (2–2.5 hours) and from Miruwa on the Pokhara–Baglung road (about 90 minutes). The Lakeside trail is steep stone steps and forest path. Walk up for sunset and stay the night, or take a taxi up for sunrise and walk down.

where_to_stay: Most visitors sleep at Lakeside and drive up before dawn, and Pokhara's hotels such as Hotel Barahi and Temple Tree Resort are 40 minutes away. To wake on the ridge, choose one of the small family guesthouses and homestays along the Sarangkot road near the viewpoint, which offer simple rooms, hot showers and dal bhat, with mountain views from the terraces. Rooms facing north are worth asking for. Book ahead in October and November, when sunrise tours fill the ridge.
tips: Check the sky from Lakeside at 4:30 am; if the stars are out, sunrise will probably be clear.
Bring a warm layer and a hat, as it is several degrees colder than the lake at dawn.
A small viewpoint entry fee is charged at the tower; carry small notes.
Paragliding operators cancel flights in cloud or strong wind, so book on a day with a spare morning after it.
Walk down rather than up if your knees can take it, and leave the climb for a cool morning.

experiences.title: Sunrise over the Annapurnas from Sarangkot
experiences.summary: A pre-dawn drive from Lakeside to the Sarangkot tower, then the slow show of first light moving along the range from Dhaulagiri to Manaslu, with Phewa and Pokhara emerging from mist below. Back at Lakeside for breakfast.
body: Your taxi leaves Lakeside around 4:45 am in October and November, a little later in winter. The road climbs in switchbacks through the dark; from the car park it is a few minutes up steps to the viewing area, where tea sellers are already frying sel roti. Find a spot facing north and wait. In October and November dozens of people gather on the tower; arrive early for a place at the rail. Tea stalls sell hot drinks for the wait, and the sky to the east begins to pale over the hills behind Pokhara.

The light comes in a sequence. Dhaulagiri, far to the west at 8,167 m, turns pink first, then Annapurna South and Annapurna I, then Machhapuchhre's twin summit directly in front, and on very clear days Manaslu and Himalchuli far to the east. Below, the valley is often full of cloud, with Phewa appearing through gaps as the sun warms it. Photographers should bring a telephoto lens for the summits and a wider lens for the valley and the lake. The light changes quickly in the first 20 minutes, so keep shooting.

Stay for half an hour after sunrise. The crowds leave quickly, the light warms, and the ridge becomes a village again: people carrying fodder, children walking to school, buffalo being milked. Walk down part of the way through the terraces if you like, and let the driver collect you lower down. Tea stalls by the car park serve sel roti and milk tea for breakfast. Most visitors are back at Lakeside by 8 am, in time for a second breakfast by the lake and a boat ride while the air is still clear.

faqs.q: What time should I leave Pokhara for Sarangkot sunrise?
faqs.a: Leave Lakeside about 60–75 minutes before sunrise: around 4:45 am in October and November, around 5:15 am in December and January, earlier in April and May. The drive takes 30–40 minutes and you then climb a few minutes of steps. Arriving early secures a good spot on the tower. Your hotel or taxi driver will know the current timing.

faqs.q: Is Sarangkot sunrise worth it in cloudy weather?
faqs.a: If the peaks are covered there is nothing to see, so check the sky before you go. From June to September views are rare. In other months, high cloud may clear just after sunrise, so wait 20–30 minutes before giving up. A clear night with stars over Lakeside usually means a good morning. Keep a spare day if sunrise matters to you.

faqs.q: How cold is it at Sarangkot at dawn?
faqs.a: At 1,600 m Sarangkot is several degrees colder than Lakeside. In December and January dawn can be near freezing, and in October and November around 8–12 °C, with a breeze on the tower. Wear a down or fleece jacket, hat and gloves. By 8 am the sun warms it quickly and you can shed layers.

experiences.title: Tandem paragliding from Sarangkot over Phewa
experiences.summary: Run off Sarangkot's slope strapped to a licensed pilot and circle on thermals above Phewa Lake with the Annapurnas behind you, then glide down to land at Lakeside. Flights last 20–30 minutes, with longer cross-country options.
body: Pokhara's paragliding works because of its geography: a south-facing ridge 800 m above a lake, warming fast in the morning sun, with a flat landing field at the water's edge. Operators collect you from Lakeside offices and drive up to the launch area just below the Sarangkot viewpoint. After a briefing and harness check you wait for the right breeze, then take a few running steps and lift off. Pilots give a short safety briefing first.

Most standard flights last 20–30 minutes, with longer cross-country flights for those who want more time in the air. Pilots ride thermals up above the launch, and on good days you can see Machhapuchhre and the Annapurnas over the ridge and Phewa directly below. Black kites and Himalayan griffon vultures often share the same thermals. Pilots often carry cameras on a pole and can film the flight for an extra fee. If you feel unwell in the air, tell the pilot: they can bring you down early and fly more gently.

The landing field is by the lake at the north end of Lakeside. Choose a registered operator with insured pilots, tell them about any health issues, and wear closed shoes and a warm layer. Flights stop in rain, low cloud or strong winds, and in the monsoon they are often cancelled for days. Book with a spare morning after the planned flight, so a weather cancellation can simply move a day. Eat a light breakfast; a full stomach and spiralling turns do not go well together.

faqs.q: Is paragliding in Pokhara safe?
faqs.a: Tandem paragliding with a registered operator and a licensed pilot has a good record in Pokhara, but it is an adventure sport with real risk. Choose established companies, check that the pilot is licensed and insured, follow the briefing and do not fly in poor weather. Check that your travel insurance covers paragliding. Operators decide on safety; respect a cancellation.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year for paragliding in Pokhara?
faqs.a: October to early December gives the clearest views and steady flying, and February to May has good thermals with more haze. Flights usually run from late morning when the slope has warmed. The monsoon, June to September, brings frequent cancellations. Book for early in your stay so a weather cancellation can be moved to another day.

faqs.q: Is there a weight or age limit for tandem paragliding?
faqs.a: Operators set their own limits, commonly a maximum body weight around 100–110 kg and a minimum age with parental consent for children. Older travellers fly regularly if they can take a few running steps at launch. Tell the operator about heart, back or pregnancy issues; they may decline. Ask the specific company before booking.

experiences.title: Hike up to Sarangkot from Lakeside
experiences.summary: Climb about 800 m from the north end of Phewa through forest, terraces and farmhouses to the Sarangkot ridge, watch the sunset over the lake and either stay the night or come down by taxi. A good leg-warmer before a trek.
body: The trail begins near the north end of Lakeside, beyond the paragliding landing area, and climbs steadily on stone steps and dirt path. The first hour is forest, cool and shaded; then the trees open onto terraced fields and scattered houses with buffalo sheds and stacked maize. Villagers use this path daily, so you will share it with schoolchildren and people carrying fodder. Watch for mules and porters on the narrow sections and give them the inside of the path.

Allow 2–2.5 hours to reach the ridge road, then follow it up to the viewpoint. On the way you pass small shops for water and tea. From the ridge Phewa spreads below, and the paragliders, if it is still early afternoon, launch just beside you. It is a fine first test of trekking boots and knees. Carry two litres of water in warm months, as the slope faces south and takes the full sun. Walking poles help on the steep stone sections, and good shoes with grip matter after rain.

Time it for the afternoon and you reach the top for sunset, when the snow peaks glow pink and Pokhara's lights come on. Then sleep in a ridge guesthouse for sunrise, or take a taxi down. Walking down the next morning through the terraces is easier on the lungs but harder on the knees. If you walk down, start soon after breakfast and you will be back at Lakeside for lunch. Ask locals at forks in the path; they are used to pointing walkers in the right direction.

faqs.q: How long does it take to hike to Sarangkot?
faqs.a: From the north end of Lakeside allow 2–2.5 hours up and about 1.5 hours down, climbing roughly 800 m on steps and paths. From Miruwa on the Pokhara–Baglung road it is about 90 minutes. Fit walkers go faster. Start in the afternoon for sunset, or early morning in hot months. Carry water; small shops on the way sell drinks.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to hike to Sarangkot?
faqs.a: No permit or guide is required, as Sarangkot is outside the Annapurna Conservation Area. Trails are well used but branch often through villages, so download an offline map or ask locals, who are used to pointing walkers uphill. Solo walkers, especially women, are better on the trail in daylight and not alone on forest sections late in the day.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight at Sarangkot?
faqs.a: Yes. Family guesthouses and homestays along the ridge road near the viewpoint offer simple rooms, hot showers and Nepali meals, with mountain views from terraces. Staying the night means you can walk out for sunrise without a 4:30 am taxi. In October and November book a day or two ahead, as sunrise groups fill the better rooms.

experiences.title: Ridge walk from Sarangkot to old Kaskikot
experiences.summary: Walk west along the ridge from Sarangkot through farmland and small settlements to Kaskikot, the hill where the kings of Kaski once kept their seat, with Phewa Lake on one side and the Annapurnas on the other.
body: After sunrise, most people drive down. Instead, follow the ridge west. A dirt road and footpaths run through maize and millet terraces, past houses with marigolds by the door and dogs asleep in the sun. Phewa Lake lies on your left, the Annapurnas on your right, and the Peace Pagoda shows white on its hill across the water. The road and paths are used by villagers, buses and the occasional jeep, so stay alert at bends.

Kaskikot was the seat of Kaski, one of the Chaubisi rajya, the twenty-four small kingdoms of the western hills, and the district still carries its name. The kings ruled Pokhara's valley from here until the Gorkha state absorbed Kaski in 1786. Little dramatic survives to the untrained eye; what you get is the position, a hilltop commanding the valley, and the reason forts were built on these ridges. Your guide can tell you which ridges were held by which small states, and how the Gorkha army moved through these hills.

Allow about two hours one way at a gentle pace with tea stops. From Kaskikot you can take a jeep or taxi back to Pokhara along the road, or continue down to the lakeshore at Pame and catch a boat or taxi to Lakeside. Bring water and sun protection: much of the ridge is unshaded. Small shops in the villages along the ridge sell tea, biscuits and soft drinks, and some families serve simple dal bhat if you ask.

faqs.q: How far is Kaskikot from Sarangkot?
faqs.a: Kaskikot lies west along the same ridge, about two hours' walk at an easy pace on dirt road and paths, with small ups and downs. There is road access, so you can arrange a taxi to collect you. It is a good morning walk after Sarangkot sunrise. Ask your guide or locals at junctions, as tracks fork through the farms.

faqs.q: What is the history of Kaskikot?
faqs.a: Kaskikot was the seat of the Kaski kingdom, one of the twenty-four small Chaubisi states that ruled the hills of western Nepal before unification. Its kings controlled the Pokhara valley and invited Newar traders to build Pokhara's market in the 1770s. Kaski was absorbed into the Gorkha state in 1786, and the district is still named after it.

faqs.q: Can I combine Kaskikot with the Panchase trek?
faqs.a: Yes. The ridge continues west from Kaskikot towards Naudanda and the Panchase hills, and some walkers link Sarangkot, Kaskikot and onward villages into a two-day route. Panchase proper is further southwest, usually reached via Bhumdi or Bhadaure. Talk to your guide about the best link and where to sleep, as homestay options change.

faqs.q: How do I get to Sarangkot from Pokhara?
faqs.a: By taxi it takes 30–40 minutes from Lakeside to the viewpoint car park on a paved road, then a short climb on steps. Most hotels can book a sunrise taxi that waits and brings you back. On foot, trails climb from the north end of Lakeside in 2–2.5 hours or from Miruwa on the Baglung road in about 90 minutes.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Sarangkot?
faqs.a: Sarangkot ridge is about 1,600 m above sea level, roughly 800 m higher than Phewa Lake. The altitude causes no health problems for healthy visitors, but it is noticeably cooler than Lakeside, especially at dawn in winter when temperatures can approach freezing. The climb on foot is steady and steep, a good fitness test before a trek.

faqs.q: Which mountains can you see from Sarangkot?
faqs.a: On clear days you see Dhaulagiri (8,167 m) to the west, the Annapurna range in front with Annapurna South, Annapurna I, Hiunchuli, Machhapuchhre and Annapurna II to IV, Lamjung Himal, and Manaslu (8,163 m) and Himalchuli to the east. Machhapuchhre's fishtail shape is clearest from here. October to February gives the best visibility.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Sarangkot viewpoint?
faqs.a: A small entry fee is charged at the viewing tower area, with different rates for Nepalis, SAARC visitors and foreigners. It is modest; carry small notes in Nepali rupees. The fee supports upkeep of the viewpoint. Fees change from time to time, so do not rely on figures in older guidebooks. No permit is needed to visit Sarangkot.

faqs.q: Is Sarangkot sunrise better than Poon Hill?
faqs.a: They are different. Sarangkot is a 40-minute drive from Pokhara and shows the range with the lake and city below. Poon Hill, at 3,210 m on a 3–4 night trek, is much closer to Dhaulagiri and Annapurna I and has a wider, higher view. If you are not trekking, Sarangkot is excellent; if you are, do both.

faqs.q: Can you stay overnight in Sarangkot?
faqs.a: Yes, several family guesthouses and homestays along the ridge road offer rooms with mountain views, hot water and home-cooked food. Staying means a sunrise without the early drive and a quiet evening with Pokhara's lights below. Facilities are simple compared with Lakeside hotels. Book ahead in October and November, the busiest months for sunrise visits.

faqs.q: What is the best time of year for Sarangkot?
faqs.a: October to February gives the clearest views, with October and November best overall and December and January cold but crisp. March and April are warmer with more haze, though early mornings are often good. From June to September, monsoon cloud hides the peaks most days and the paths are muddy, though the terraces are very green.

faqs.q: Is Sarangkot suitable for elderly travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, if you go by car. The taxi reaches a car park close to the viewpoint, and from there it is a few minutes up steps to the tower, with railings. Take it slowly and wear warm clothes. The walk up from Lakeside is steep and better suited to those used to hill walking. Midday visits avoid the dawn cold.

faqs.q: How long does the paragliding flight from Sarangkot last?
faqs.a: Standard tandem flights last 20–30 minutes in the air, and the full trip including pick-up, the drive to the launch, briefing and waiting for wind takes 2–3 hours. Longer cross-country flights of around an hour are offered by some operators. Flights depend on weather and may be delayed or cancelled; book with a spare day.
